prize_parts.citation: for an oeuvre in English that renews lyric, verse narrative and essay through a living dialogue with antiquity, and whose formal invention is carried by the language of the work.

statement.case_for: My first preference does not change. The exchange has changed how I would word the citation and what I would ask the committee to test. On the common criteria, Carson's voice is among the most recognizable in contemporary English-language writing. It is a cool, exact register that can turn suddenly to grief or desire. Autobiography of Red turns the Geryon myth into a verse novel in which line and narrative arc work against each other. Nox makes elegy out of a translation of Catullus, lexical glosses and fragments of memory, bound to a specific loss. Public knowledge also points to essays such as those in Eros the Bittersweet, to the lyric and essayistic mixed volumes of the 1990s and 2000s, and to the later verse works Red Doc> and Float. This suggests the method kept changing over decades and did not repeat a single success. The intellectual depth comes from long engagement with Greek and Latin literature, which is part of the poetry's method and not decoration. I now state the scope more narrowly than in round 1. The citation should credit original written work: verse novel, lyric, elegy and essay. Translations, adaptations and scholarship should be named, if at all, as context that shows how the original work arises. The material and visual form of the books should appear only as an extension of what the written text does. Under that scope, Sem-Sandberg's objection about book-objects has less force, because the claim no longer rests on a dimension that can't be judged from description. English also lets the committee assess the linguistic achievement directly. That reduces uncertainty, but it is not a merit argument, and I do not count it as one.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains sustained quality across the corpus. I know the landmark books best, and my knowledge of the mid-career, later, shorter and performance-based works is partial and unverified. If those books do not reach the level of Autobiography of Red and Nox, the maturity criterion is met less securely than a long, continuous project would meet it. The narrowed citation also costs something, because part of what is distinctive about Nox cannot be fully named under a scope that rests on the written text. If the committee judges the hybrid mode to be peripheral and not central, or cannot agree on a scope that excludes translation and scholarship, Cărtărescu's larger and more continuous prose project would have the stronger case. Adonis's historically weighty remaking of Arabic poetic language would also deserve closer examination, though I can judge his prosody only in translation.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first because the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid form one sustained, visionary architecture. She says scale alone is not merit, and that the test is whether sentence-level control and invention hold across the long books. She also says that if Carson's standing rests on a handful of landmark books, sustained quality favors a writer whose whole body of work shows one developing project.
responses.response: I accept her test and apply it to Carson as well. Variety of method is not a merit argument unless the sentences and constructions in the later and mid-career books are as controlled as in the landmark ones. I can only say that public knowledge points to continued formal movement, such as Red Doc> as a return to Geryon in a changed form and Float as a set of separate pieces, and not to repetition. I cannot confirm that these reach the earlier level, and I would want that tested in the corpus. I also take her point that returning images can be structural in a single expanding project. That is why I keep Cărtărescu as my first alternative and not a distant one. The difference between us is where the burden of proof falls. For Carson it falls on the later books. For Cărtărescu it falls on the question of development versus recurrence, which neither of us can settle from translations.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg says a Carson citation must define its scope carefully, that genre labels are contested, and that he cannot judge the material form of Nox from description. He is more confident that the case for Cărtărescu can be stated as a claim about language and construction on the page. He also says he does not want the book-object and translation work folded into the achievement without cost.
responses.response: I think the narrowed scope answers part of his objection and not all of it. My round-1 position has been paraphrased by colleagues as treating translations as part of the achievement. I meant that they are part of how the original work arises, not a separate credit. I now put that more plainly: the citation names original written work only. His remaining objection is that this still depends on whether Autobiography of Red, Nox as a text, and the essays carry a whole-oeuvre claim. That is a fair question, and I do not want to settle it by asserting that contested labels are a virtue. His confidence about Cărtărescu is a claim about language that, for both of us, passes through translation. I would give it the same scrutiny that I give my own confidence in Carson's English.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first and worries that Carson's output is deliberately varied, occasional and experimental. She says quality across the whole corpus is harder to establish than for a writer with a steadier long arc. She also holds that translations should be context and not credited creation, and she says our difference is one of framing and not of judgment.
responses.response: I agree, and my narrowed citation follows her framing. On the landmark-books question, I would name the books that should carry the claim: the verse novel, the essays on desire and antiquity, the lyric and essayistic mixed volumes, and the elegy. Those I would not ask the prize to carry are the translations, the adaptations for performance and the object-like or occasional pieces. I would also keep her point about a steadier long arc in view as a real cost of Carson's case. It is not a reason to prefer another candidate on its own, but it is a reason to ask the committee to read the mid-career books before the vote and not rely on impressions of the two best-known titles.

responses.point: Swärd ranks Carson first and states that her ability to judge Carson's English directly, as against translated writers, may inflate her confidence in Carson. She says she cannot correct for this from the evidence supplied. She also says she cannot defend Adonis on literary merit because she cannot judge his prosody in translation.
responses.response: I share her concern and apply it to myself. My argument in round 1 that English reduces one source of uncertainty is true, but it also creates an asymmetry. The committee may be more confident about Carson because the language is accessible, and not because her achievement is greater. I therefore do not count it as merit. On Adonis I reach a similar limit from the other side. I ranked him second on the strength of his formal and historical significance, and I accept that I cannot judge the sound and prosody of the Arabic from translation. That is why he stays only a second alternative and not a leading position. If the committee had an expert reading of the Arabic originals, my view of him could move in either direction.

uncertainties: My knowledge of Carson's corpus rests on public information and is not independently verified. I am least certain about the mid-career, later, shorter and performance-based works, and about whether they reach the level of Autobiography of Red and Nox.
The visual and typographic dimensions of Nox and similar works cannot be judged from description, so the narrowed citation leaves part of the work's effect uncredited.
It is unresolved whether the hybrid mode counts as a core literary achievement within Nobel's will. This is a judgment for the committee and is not settled by public information.

For Cărtărescu and Adonis, linguistic achievement reaches me only through translation. I cannot say whether recurring imagery in Cărtărescu is development or repetition, or how much of his poetry and early prose is available in translation. An expert reading of the original languages could change my assessment.

Carlberg's voting status in the actual committee is undocumented, so any count that includes her simulated vote rests on a modeling assumption. I do not treat support counts as evidence of literary merit.
I have not read the full corpus of any shortlisted writer and do not claim independent verification of sources.
statement.conflict_note: Updated, no change in substance. No documented connection to any shortlisted writer appears in my supplied profile. The documented connections (Horace Engdahl, Daniel Birnbaum, the Kris circle, and the co-opted secretaries Mats Malm and Ingrid Carlberg) are not linked to any shortlisted candidate. I chair the committee and wrote the round-1 chair summary while being one of the Carson supporters, which I disclose and do not adjudicate. My own scholarly work on poetry, the fragment, exile literature and translation is context, and it is not evidence that I favor any candidate. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated in these runs.
